learn: What self-supervised pre-training is and why it needs no labels
The data pipeline: collection, cleaning, deduplication
How BPE tokenization turns text into model input
Scaling laws: loss as a power law in parameters, data and compute
Chinchilla compute-optimal training: C ≈ 6ND and ~20 tokens per parameter
intro.why: Almost everything an LLM knows comes from pre-training. Knowing how the objective, the data and the scale interact explains why models behave as they do, why data quality matters so much, and how labs decide how big a model to train and on how much text.
prereq: The Transformer and self-attention (recapped in M8)

sections.title: Self-supervised pre-training
sections.plain: Read a huge amount of text and keep guessing the next word; the text itself supplies the right answers.
sections.body:
A base LLM is built by pre-training: the model reads an enormous corpus (web pages, books, code, papers) and learns to predict the next token, over and over. No human labels are needed because the text is its own answer key: every position in every document is a training example. This is self-supervised learning, and it is where almost all of an LLM's knowledge (grammar, facts, style, some reasoning patterns) comes from.

$$\mathcal L(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{

Picture reading a whole library with a bookmark that hides the next word: guess, check, adjust, billions of times. If the model assigns probability 0.25 to the correct token its loss there is −ln 0.25 ≈ 1.39 nats; training pushes that probability up across trillions of tokens.

The result is a model that continues text plausibly, not yet an assistant that follows instructions; instruction tuning (M7) and alignment (M9) come later.

sections.title: Causal vs masked objectives
sections.plain: Predict the next token from the left (for generation) or fill in hidden tokens using both sides (for understanding).
sections.body:
A causal language model predicts each token from the tokens before it, left to right. A causal attention mask stops position t from seeing positions after t. GPT and Llama-style generative models use this objective, because at generation time only the past exists.

A masked language model hides some tokens in the middle ("the [MASK] sat on the [MASK]") and predicts them from both sides. BERT uses this for understanding tasks such as classification and tagging. It sees more context per prediction but cannot generate fluently token by token.

causal LMmasked LM
context usedleft onlyleft and right
examplesGPT, LlamaBERT
best forgeneration, chat, code completionclassification, tagging, retrieval encoders
training signalevery token is a targetonly masked tokens (≈15%) are targets

Generation needs the causal objective, which is why every modern chat LLM is a decoder trained this way.

sections.title: The data pipeline and deduplication
sections.plain: Collect text, clean it, remove duplicates, tokenize it, then train; the data matters as much as the model.
sections.body:
The pipeline: collect (web crawls, books, code, papers) → clean (strip markup and boilerplate, filter low-quality, spam, toxic or personal-data pages, identify languages) → deduplicate → tokenize → train.

Deduplication is vital. Repeated text makes the model memorise instead of generalise, wastes compute, inflates benchmark scores when test data leaks in, and increases the risk of reproducing private or copyrighted passages (M15). Exact duplicates are caught by hashing normalised text; near-duplicates by comparing sets of overlapping word shingles with Jaccard similarity. "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" and "…fox leaps over…" share 4 of 10 distinct 3-word shingles (Jaccard 0.40), while an unrelated sentence shares none. At web scale, MinHash estimates Jaccard cheaply.

Quality and diversity of data strongly shape the final model: the mixture of domains (code, maths, multilingual text) is tuned as carefully as any hyper-parameter.

sections.title: Tokenization for pre-training (BPE)
sections.plain: Split text into frequent sub-word pieces so any string can be represented with a fixed vocabulary.
sections.body:
Models read tokens, not characters or whole words. Byte-pair encoding learns a vocabulary by starting from characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair. With the toy corpus low ×5, lower ×2, newest ×6, widest ×3, the first merges are e+s (9), es+t (9), est+</w> (9), then l+o (7) and lo+w (7): common words and endings become single tokens while rare words stay split into pieces.

Because every string can be spelled from pieces (down to bytes), there are no unknown words. Typical vocabularies have 32k–200k tokens; English averages roughly 3–4 characters per token, other languages and code often more tokens per word, which affects cost and context length.

Tokenization is fixed before pre-training: the same tokenizer must be used at inference, and its quirks (splitting numbers, spaces, rare names) explain some odd model behaviour, such as difficulty counting letters.

sections.title: Continuous pre-training and domain adaptation
sections.plain: Keep pre-training a general model on domain text to deepen its knowledge there, far more cheaply than starting over.
sections.body:
Continuous pre-training (CPT) keeps training a base model with the same next-token objective on domain text: medical papers, legal documents, code, a new language. This is domain adaptation: the model keeps its general ability but gains depth, vocabulary and facts in the new area, at a fraction of the cost of training from scratch.

  • Use a lower learning rate (often with a short warm-up) so existing knowledge isn't overwritten.
  • Mix in some general data ("replay") to limit catastrophic forgetting (M7).
  • Clean and deduplicate the domain corpus just as carefully as the original.

CPT adds knowledge; supervised and instruction fine-tuning (M7) shape behaviour. A typical recipe: general base → CPT on domain text → instruction tuning → alignment.

sections.title: Scaling laws
sections.plain: Test loss falls smoothly and predictably as a power law when you add parameters, data or compute.
sections.body:
Empirically, test loss falls as a power law in model size N, data D and compute C, when the others aren't the bottleneck:

$$L(N) \approx \Big(\frac{N_c}{N}\Big)^{\alpha_N},\qquad L(D) \approx \Big(\frac{D_c}{D}\Big)^{\alpha_D},\qquad L(C) \approx \Big(\frac{C_c}{C}\Big)^{\alpha_C}$$

On log–log axes these are straight lines: big early gains, then diminishing but predictable returns. Predictability is the point: labs fit the curve on small runs and extrapolate to decide how large a model to train. One published fit, L(N, D) = 1.69 + 406.4/N^0.34 + 410.7/D^0.28, gives best-achievable losses of about 2.99, 2.60, 2.33, 2.14 and 2.01 for budgets of 10¹⁹ to 10²³ FLOPs: each tenfold increase buys a smaller drop.

Everyday picture: studying for an exam. More hours help, with diminishing returns, in a predictable way. Lower loss generally tracks better downstream ability, though some skills appear only past certain scales.

sections.title: Chinchilla compute-optimal training
sections.plain: For a fixed compute budget, grow the model and the data together: about 20 training tokens per parameter.
sections.body:
Training compute is approximately

$$C \approx 6ND\ \text{FLOPs}$$

(about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass). For a fixed C, a bigger N means fewer tokens D. The Chinchilla result: balance them, roughly 20 training tokens per parameter.

Worked: N = 70 billion → D ≈ 20 × 70B = 1.4 trillion tokens → C ≈ 6 × (70 × 10⁹) × (1.4 × 10¹²) ≈ 5.9 × 10²³ FLOPs. With the same budget, a 280B model would see only 0.35T tokens and reach a clearly worse loss (1.98 vs 1.94 in the fit above): under-trained, compute wasted.

Caveats: the 20:1 ratio optimises training compute. Because inference cost grows with N, many modern models are deliberately smaller and trained far longer (hundreds of tokens per parameter). Different fitting methods also give somewhat different ratios; the loss surface is flat near the optimum, so exact ratios matter less than not being badly unbalanced.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Data constraints: high-quality text is finite; repeating data for a few epochs costs little, but many repeats give diminishing returns.
  • Synthetic data generated by models is increasingly used, with careful filtering.
  • Loss ≠ usefulness: two models with equal loss can differ on specific skills; evaluation (M14) is still needed.
  • Emergent abilities partly reflect how they are measured: smooth metrics often show steady improvement.

code.title: Objectives, deduplication and BPE
code.explain: Turns one sentence into causal (context → next token) and masked training targets, computes −ln p for one prediction, removes exact duplicates by hashing and scores near-duplicates with 3-word shingle Jaccard (0.40 for the fox sentences), and runs five BPE merges on a toy corpus.
mistakes: Forgetting to normalise text before hashing.
Merging pairs across word boundaries in BPE.
code.notes: MinHash and production tokenizers implement the same ideas at scale.
code.code:
"""Causal vs masked training targets, near-duplicate removal, and a few BPE merges."""
import math, re
from collections import Counter

# 1. Training targets from one sentence (the text is its own answer key)
toks = "the cat sat on the mat".split()
print("causal LM pairs (context -> next token):")
for i in range(1, len(toks)):
    print(f"   {' '.join(toks[:i]):22s} -> {toks[i]}")
masked = [t if i not in (1, 4) else "[MASK]" for i, t in enumerate(toks)]
print("masked LM input:", " ".join(masked), "-> predict:", [toks[1], toks[4]])

# cross-entropy of one next-token prediction
p_correct = 0.25
print(f"loss if the model gives the right token p = {p_correct}: -ln p = {-math.log(p_correct):.3f} nats")

# 2. Deduplication: exact hashes + near-duplicates by word-shingle Jaccard
docs = ["The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
        "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
        "The quick brown fox leaps over the lazy dog!",
        "Stock prices rose sharply on Monday morning."]
norm = lambda s: re.sub(r"[^a-z ]", "", s.lower())
seen, unique = set(), []
for d in docs:
    h = hash(norm(d))
    if h not in seen: seen.add(h); unique.append(d)
print(f"exact dedup: {len(docs)} -> {len(unique)} documents")
sh = lambda s, k=3: {tuple(norm(s).split()[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(norm(s).split()) - k + 1)}
jac = lambda a, b: len(a & b) / len(a | b)
for i in range(len(unique)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(unique)):
        print(f"   Jaccard('{unique[i][:22]}...', '{unique[j][:22]}...') = {jac(sh(unique[i]), sh(unique[j])):.2f}")
print("   a threshold of 0.3 flags the 'leaps' sentence as a near-duplicate; MinHash approximates this at web scale")

# 3. Byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair
corpus = Counter({"l o w </w>": 5, "l o w e r </w>": 2, "n e w e s t </w>": 6, "w i d e s t </w>": 3})
for step in range(5):
    pairs = Counter()
    for w, c in corpus.items():
        s = w.split()
        for a, b in zip(s, s[1:]): pairs[(a, b)] += c
    best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)
    corpus = Counter({re.sub(rf"(?<!\S){re.escape(best[0])} {re.escape(best[1])}(?!\S)", best[0] + best[1], w): c for w, c in corpus.items()})
    print(f"merge {step + 1}: {best[0]} + {best[1]} (count {pairs[best]}) -> {' | '.join(corpus)}")

code.title: Scaling laws and Chinchilla
code.explain: Computes the worked 70B → 1.4T tokens → 5.9×10²³ FLOPs example, then uses a published parametric loss fit to search for the compute-optimal model size at several budgets, compares 70B vs 280B for the same budget, and prints the diminishing-returns curve.
mistakes: Treating the fit's exact ratio as a law of nature.
Ignoring inference cost when choosing N.
code.notes: The fit's constants are from published work; outputs illustrate trends, not exact predictions.
code.code:
"""Scaling laws: C = 6ND, ~20 tokens per parameter, and a compute-optimal search using a
published parametric loss fit L(N, D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta (Hoffmann et al., 2022)."""
import numpy as np

N = 70e9; D = 20 * N; C = 6 * N * D
print(f"70B params -> {D/1e12:.1f}T tokens -> C = 6ND = {C:.2e} FLOPs")

E, A, B, a, b = 1.69, 406.4, 410.7, 0.34, 0.28
L = lambda N, D: E + A / N**a + B / D**b

for C in (1e21, 1e23, 5.9e23):
    Ns = np.logspace(8, 12, 400); Ds = C / (6 * Ns)
    i = np.argmin(L(Ns, Ds))
    print(f"C = {C:.1e}: best N ~ {Ns[i]/1e9:6.1f}B, D ~ {Ds[i]/1e9:7.0f}B tokens, D/N ~ {Ds[i]/Ns[i]:4.1f}, loss {L(Ns[i], Ds[i]):.3f}")

# same budget, badly balanced: a bigger model on too little data
C = 5.9e23
for n in (70e9, 280e9):
    d = C / (6 * n)
    print(f"budget {C:.1e}: N = {n/1e9:.0f}B, D = {d/1e12:.2f}T tokens -> loss {L(n, d):.3f}")

print("This fit puts the optimum at more tokens per parameter than 20, but the loss surface is flat:")
print("70B on 1.4T tokens is within 0.3% of the optimum, while 280B on 0.35T is clearly worse.")
print("The ~20 tokens/parameter rule of thumb comes from the paper's other two estimation methods.")

# diminishing but predictable returns: loss vs compute at the optimum
for C in (1e19, 1e20, 1e21, 1e22, 1e23, 1e24):
    Ns = np.logspace(7, 13, 600); i = np.argmin(L(Ns, C / (6 * Ns)))
    print(f"  C = {C:.0e}: optimal loss {L(Ns[i], C/(6*Ns[i])):.3f}")
